newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court upholds complaint on cross-border profit transfers.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds complaint on cross-border profit transfers.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday Community rules exempting profit transfers between parent companies and subsidiaries from withholding tax did not allow states to unilaterally tighten restrictions.

This issue was raised in the context of a challenge by three Dutch companies against the German Federal Finance Authority, which refused to recognise a witholding exemption for profits from their German-based subsidiaries.
The directive harmonising taxation of subsidiaries requires a parent company to own at least 25 percent of its subsidiary continuously for a minumum of two years to qualify for the exemption.
Parent companies Denkavit, VITIC and Voormeer argued that they did not have to wait until the end of the two-year period to qualify for the exemption.

The court agreed, noting the intent of the directive is to encourage cross-border holdings. "Member states cannot ... unilaterally introduce restrictive measures such as the requirement ... that a minimum holding period must already have been completed when the profits in respect of which the tax advantage is sought are distributed," the court said.
However, the court said member states were not obliged to grant the exemption immediately and should create detailed arrangements to ensure compliance.

"On no view are those states obliged under the directive to grant the advantage immediately on the basis of a unilateral undertaking by the parent company to observe the minimum holding period," the court said.
The court determined that parent companies have standing to challenge member state tax decisions, taken under articles 3 and 5 of the directive, directly before national courts.

Denkavit asked the court to rule that Germany's refusal to grant an exemption from withholding tax gave rise to a serious breach of Community law, subject to compensable damage claims in national courts.

To determine liability on the part of a member state, the court reviewed its "sufficiently serious" test laid out in earlier decisions. The court has said that in order for there to be a serious breach, the clarity and precison of the rule breached must be considered.
The court found no serious breach, noting most member states had interpreted the directive in the same way as Germany and no earlier court ruling had interpreted this provision.
EXCERPTS FROM THE JUDGMENT
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: German)
"Harmonisation of tax legislation - Taxation of company profits - Parent companies and subsidiaries"
17 October 1996
In Joined Cases C-283/94, C-291/94 and C-292/94
Reference by the Finanzgericht Koln (Germany) for preliminary rulings in the proceedings pending before that court between
Denkavit Internationaal BV (C-283/94)
VITIC Amsterdam BV (C_291/94) and
Voormeer BV (C-292/94)
and
Bundesamt fur Finanzen

on the interpretation of articles 3 and 5 of Council directive 90/435/EEC of 23 July 1990 on the common system of taxation applicable in the case of parent companies and subsidiaries of different member states (OJ 1990 L 225, p. 6)
THE COURT hereby rules

1. A member state may not make grant of the tax advantage provided for in article 5(1) of Council directive 90/435/EEC of 23 July 1990 on the common system of taxation applicable in the case of parent companies and subsidiaries of different member states subject to the condition that, at the moment when profits are distributed, the parent company must have held a minimum of 25 per cent of the capital of the subsidiary for a period at least equal to that set by that member state pursuant to article 3(2) of the directive. It is for the member states to draw up rules for ensuring compliance with this minimum period, in accordance wth the procedures laid down in their domestic law. On no view are those States obliged under the directive to grant the advantage immediately on the basis of a unilateral undertaking by the parent company to observe the minimum holding period.

2. Where a member state has exercised the option provided for in article 3(2) of the directive, parent companies may rely directly on the rights conferred by article 5(1) and (3) of the directive before national courts, if those companies observe the holding period set by that member state.

3. Community law does not require a member state which, when transposing the directive, stipulated that the minimum holding period set pursuant to article 3(2) must be completed at the time when the profits that are the subject of the tax advantage afforded by article 5 are distributed, to compensate the parent company for damage which it may have incurred by reason of the error thus made.
